extracted.intended_audience: natural philosophers and industrial practitioners (17th‑century chemists, manufacturers, salt-makers, brewers, and farmers)
extracted.subtask_short: manufacture of alum, copperas, salt, maize
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural production and quality criteria for early-modern manufacture of alum, kelp, copperas (green vitriol), salt, and for maize cultivation and malting; aimed at practitioners and scientific readers describing what good vs bad material/process looks like and how to manage operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quality of pit liquor for alum
rubrics_metrics.description: "That liquor which comes whitest from the pits is the best."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Whiteness of liquor from pits is used as primary quality indicator; dark, muddy consistence indicates bad mineral or incorrect calcining (over- or under-calcining).

rubrics_metrics.name: Urine quality for alum precipitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Use urine to cast off slam and to prevent kelp-lees hardening alum too much; best urine 'comes from poor labouring people, who drink but little strong liquor.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Check urine for sea-water adulteration by adding some to boiling liquor: good urine will 'work like yest [yeast] put to beer or ale'; mixed (with sea-water) urine 'will stir no more than so much water.' Adjust volume of urine according to 'goodness of the liquor' (more urine required for nitrous/red liquor).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator tests during alum boiling
rubrics_metrics.description: During boiling the liquor, 'if good, will in boiling seem greasy at the top: if nitrous it will be thick, muddy, and red.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use surface appearance during boil to assess nitrous contamination; nitrous liquor requires different handling (more urine, stronger kelp-lees).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and management of "mothers" in alum boilers
rubrics_metrics.description: Save the liquor 'which comes from the alum, or wherein the alum shoots, which they call mothers' and use mothers to fill two thirds of boilers with one third fresh liquor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Re-use mothers to reduce fresh liquor consumption; mothers require kelp-lees to effect separation; boil and refresh every ~5 days until liquor evaporates/turns to alum and slam.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cooler standing time for alum crystallization
rubrics_metrics.description: In temperate weather the liquor stands 4 days in the cooler; 'The second day the alum begins to strike, gather and harden about the sides, and at the bottom of the cooler.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not let liquor stand above 4 days (they say it would turn to copperas); hot weather lengthens cooling, frost strikes too soon and mixes impurities causing 'double the quantity' but foul output; monitor weather when cooling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of kelp-lees in alum manufacture
rubrics_metrics.description: Kelp-lees are used to separate nitre and slam (settling) and to assist mothers in producing alum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add kelp-lees (quantity adjusted) to cause slam/nitre to sink in settlers; in boilers of green liquor kelp-lees may be unnecessary, but when mothers are used kelp-lees are needed to effect separation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Washing and roaching alum before market
rubrics_metrics.description: Alum taken from sides/bottom is washed with used water (~12 pounds weight), then 'roached' by melting/boiling in a pan, emptied into a cask to stand 10 days and then fit for market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Washing removes foulness; roaching (brief melt/boil and repose) conditions product for sale; follow specified weights and resting time to reach market quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kelp production from tangle sea-weed
rubrics_metrics.description: Kelp is made of a sea-weed called tangle: dried it burns and runs like pitch; when cold and hard it is beaten to ashes, steeped in water, and the lees drawn off to about 2 pounds weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Process kelp to a consistent lees weight for use in alum/copperas processes; kelp-lees quality affects separation efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selection of copperas-stones (martial pyrites)
rubrics_metrics.description: Best stones are 'of a bright shining silver colour'; next best 'rusty deep yellow'; worst are 'dull or umber colour' with gravel and dirt.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer bright silver-coloured stones for highest quality copperas; avoid stones containing gravel, dirt or impurities (lower yield and quality).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bed preparation for copperas extraction
rubrics_metrics.description: Beds are rammed with strong clay then rubble chalk with a wooden trough in the middle to collect liquor; stones laid about 2 feet thick; beds may need 5–6 years before significant liquor yield.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct beds to prevent leakage, slope to trough, board and cover trough; do not over-water (watering retards ripening); refresh beds every ~4 years by laying new stones and mixing in old fermented earth to hasten ripening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cistern construction and maintenance for copperas
rubrics_metrics.description: Cisterns of strong oaken boards, well joined and chalked, divided in middle so any side may be mended; prevent drainage through beds or cistern.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure cistern impermeability; dividing aids repair; leaky cisterns reduce liquor yield and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical tests of brine/copperas liquor strength (egg and weight tests)
rubrics_metrics.description: 'J 4 penny weight is rich: or an egg being put into the liquor, the higher it swims above the liquor, the stronger it is... Within one minute after an egg is put in, the ambient liquor will boil and froth; and in 3 minutes the shell will be quite worn off.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use simple empirical measures (weights and egg float/attack tests) to assess liquor strength and corrosiveness; handle accordingly (fabric damage indicates high acidity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Iron addition and furnace design for copperas boiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with ~100 lb old iron in lead trough; add iron gradually (total ~1500 lb) during boiling; order furnace so heat reaches all parts; Sir Nicolas Crisp's 'heater' vessel keeps replacement liquor hot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continuous supply of iron prevents copperas gathering and melting on the boiler bottom; avoid pumping cold liquor directly into boiler (use pre-heated supply) to maintain boil and speed production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indicator of copperas boiling readiness and cooler handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Test by taking small quantity into shallow pan and observing time to crust about sides; when drawn to cooler copperas gathers/shoots 14–15 days, sticks to sides as bright green and bottom as foul dirty colour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use pan-test to judge completeness; separate deposits from cleaner side-growth (bright green) vs bottom (dirtier) and handle accordingly; transfer remaining liquor to be boiled again.

rubrics_metrics.name: Danger of boiling copperas without iron
rubrics_metrics.description: Copperas may be boiled without iron but 'with difficulty' and the boiler may be in danger of melting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer iron addition when boiling copperas to avoid damaging boilers and to increase yield of vitriolic salt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salt-pit and brine source characterization (Droitwich)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pits produce brines of different strengths (first-man, middle-man, last-man); strength measured by quart weight (e.g., 29 oz yields >1/4 salt).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Categorize and use brines according to strength; stronger brines yield more salt per volume, choose pit accordingly for production goals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vat/pan construction for salt boiling
rubrics_metrics.description: Vats made of lead cast into flat plate then sides beaten up, set on brick ovens with grates; lead preferred because forged/cast iron corrodes or breaks under strong brine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose material resistant to brine corrosion (lead pans used); iron pans tested and found wanting—forge iron corrodes, cast iron breaks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarifying salt with egg whites
rubrics_metrics.description: Clarify brine with whites of eggs: a quarter of a white beaten with a gallon or two of brine, a small quantity of froth put in each vat raises scum; 'the white of one egg clarifying 20 bushels of salt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use whipped egg-white froth as clarifier to remove dust/scum and produce white salt; avoid clarifying with blood (gives ill savour).

rubrics_metrics.name: Granulation control for salt (rosin addition)
rubrics_metrics.description: For granulating, add a small quantity of rosin to brine to make smaller grains; otherwise strong brine will form large grains (bay-salt-like) if not frequently stirred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust rosin addition to attain desired grain size (more rosin -> finer grain; additional rosin for 'salt loaves').

rubrics_metrics.name: Categorization and intended uses of salt grades
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple sorts: white salt (finest), clod-salt (adheres to vat bottoms; strongest; used for bacon and runnet-pots), knockings (from stales), scrapings (coarse, mixed with dross), pigeon salt (from cracks), salt loaves (fine).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sort and market/use salts according to quality and strength: clod/knockings for heavy salting, scrapings for poorer customers, loaves for fine sale. Recognize that clod-salt is very strong and affects meat colouring/texture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Storage and keeping quality of produced salt
rubrics_metrics.description: Our salt is 'not so apt to dissolve' as Cheshire salt and keeps well without fire; brine clarity means little need to clarify except dust.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properly clarified and dried salt stores longer; choose production/clarifying methods that yield less-dissolving product when long keeping is desired.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planting dates for maize
rubrics_metrics.description: Maize is planted between middle of March and beginning of June; most commonly from middle of April to middle of May; Mohawks corn can be planted in June and still ripen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select planting date appropriate to variety and local climate; later-maturing varieties permit later planting in northerly regions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Planting spacing and sowing method for maize
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant in rows about 5 or 6 feet apart; open earth 3–4 inches deep and put in 4–5 grains a little distant from one another, then cover.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Spacing allows for hoeing and cultivation; sow multiple grains per station to allow for losses to birds/rodents; thin/leave multiple seedlings (2–3) if they grow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cultivation/weeding and hilling schedule for maize
rubrics_metrics.description: When corn up a hand's length, cut up weeds and loosen earth with a broad hoe; when stalk starts to grow high draw a little earth about it and form small hill at ear emergence; repeat weeding and ploughing as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Regular early weeding and hilling reduces competition and encourages root spread; after hilling little is necessary until harvest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harvest and storage of maize ears to avoid spoilage
rubrics_metrics.description: After gathering, strip husks immediately (unless laid thin) or weave ears into traces and hang on stages to keep through winter; if not stripped and left thick, it will heat, grow mouldy, and sprout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dry and store ears properly (hung or dried on mats) to prevent heating and sprouting; native methods include drying on mats and storing in ground-lined holes with withered grass.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of fish/aloofes as fertilizer
rubrics_metrics.description: On poor or worn ground Indians put two or three fishes (aloofes) under or adjacent to each corn-hill, sometimes doubling crop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use available fish waste/garbage (cod heads) as local fertilizer to boost yields on poor soils.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intercropping companion plants with maize
rubrics_metrics.description: Plant beans at each corn-hill (stalks serve as poles), plant squashes/pumpkins in vacant places and sprinkle turnip-seed between hills after last weeding for additional crop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use companion planting to intensively load ground and obtain multiple crops from same area; beans climb stalks and pumpkins occupy space between hills.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparation and uses of maize as food and for beer
rubrics_metrics.description: Maize prepared by parching in ashes, bruising in mortars, making samp (rice-sized meal boiled with milk/butter/sugar), or converted to bread (requires specific dough consistency and baking technique); beer may be made from bread or by malting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use appropriate processing per intended product: for bread avoid very stiff paste; for samp sift and winnow hulls and boil gently; for beer either mash bread lumps or malt grain specially.

rubrics_metrics.name: Malting maize—required sprouting behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: To make good malt of maize it must 'sprout out both ways, i. e. both root and blade, to a great length, of a finger at least.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induce and permit extensive double-direction sprouting (root and blade) by laying grain covered on earth for 10–14 days; then take up, shake earth off and dry to produce mellow, floury malt suitable for making wholesome beer.

rubrics_metrics.name: Barley selection and storage for malt (Scotland)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two barley kinds: four-row (common) and two-row (best malt). Newly threshed barley makes better malt; barley overheated in stacks will not make good malt. Keeping barley in chaff preserves it longer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer two-row and recently threshed barley; store barley in chaff on boarded floors, turned occasionally; avoid over-heating during storage to prevent poor malting quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Steeping and coming-heap management for barley malting
rubrics_metrics.description: Steep 8 bolls in water until water bright reddish (~3 days, variable); after draining, heap 20–24 inches deep as 'coming heap' for ~40 hours; watch first 15–16 hours—turn within an hour after roots have fully put forth to prevent blade/spire growth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Control steep time by season and grain characteristics; monitor heap closely and turn promptly when root development reaches desired stage—if blade sprouting begins malt is spoiled in taste and strength.
